newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices slip as heating oil crunch eases.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices slip as heating oil crunch eases.

text.p: Oil prices extended losses in cautious early trade on Wednesday following news that a big heating oil stock shortfall in the United States is easing after underpinning the world market for months.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea for January delivery hit a low of $22.89 a barrel during the morning, down 40 cents from Tuesday's close when it settled a hefty 81 cents down on the day.
After the market closed on Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute (API) said stocks of U.S. crude oil, distillates -- mostly heating oil -- and gasoline rose last week.

The rise was largely the result of increased refinery production and a 1.5 million barrel per day (bpd) jump in imports. U.S. heating oil stocks in the key Northeast region remained 29 percent below last year's levels but better than the 40 percent shortfall seen earlier this year.

Stock building, mild weather forecasts for the U.S. northeast, the world's largest heating oil consumer, and the resumption of Iraqi oil flows after a six-year absence, has sliced some $1.50 off the oil price since last week.

"Sentiment in the complex has clearly become more negative with the (mild) weather not helping...there are a number of bearish fundamental influences weighing" in, said brokers GNI in their daily report.
But some traders said it was too early into the winter to sell the market short since heating oil inventories on both sides of the Atlantic are still down from 1995 levels.

"Technically, it is under pressure right now but it can easily bounce back. The winter is just beginning and the underlying tone is bullish," said Oystein Berentsen, head of international crude oil trading at the Norwegian state oil company Statoil.

Berentsen said the market could easily absorb the 500,000 to 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude exports which should hit the market soon now that the much-delayed U.N. food-for-oil plan has been approved.
"Iraqi oil could not have hit the market at a better time. The demand is there," Berentsen said.
On Tuesday, Iraqi strongman Saddam Hussein ceremoniously hit the switch which should have sent 650,000 bpd of Iraqi crude through a pipeline to Turkey's Ceyhan port on the Mediterranean.

A technical glitch meant that no oil actually made it to Turkey, although the state-run Turkish Anatolian news agency said the oil flow began around 1000 GMT on Wednesday at a rate of 350,000 barrels per day.
The absence of Iraqi crude from tight oil markets was partly the reason why prices shot to a near six-year high in October when the U.N. oil-for-food deal was postponed from September.
Crude oil prices remain on average around $3.0 a barrel higher than this time last year.
Under the U.N. deal signed in May, Iraq will be allowed to sell $2.0 billion worth of crude oil for six months to buy food and medicines under strict U.N. supervision.
Iraq said it would pump 650,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil through its pipeline to Ceyhan and through its Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr under the U.N. plan cleared on Monday.

Other than Turkey, no firm buyers have emerged from among the more than 50 oil company executives Iraq said had flocked to Baghdad to conclude term deals, but French companies Elf and Total are said to be close to inking contracts.

Iraq, before the Gulf War the second biggest oil producer in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) after Saudi Arabia, produced 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude in July 1990.
